intro_en: A special segment of the Israel National Trail, linking the desert fringe and the southern Hebron Hills with the desert and the Arad Valley. Wonderful scenery all year round and colourful blooms in spring.
character_en: (From north to south) A gentle climb at first, then a long descent of moderate difficulty to Drijat. Afterwards, flat walking between Drijat and Arad.
transport_en: The community of Har Amasa (infrequent service). Tel Arad Junction. The entrance to Arad.
important_en: Har Amasa is higher than Jerusalem. On winter days with a strong wind it can be very cold, and with a little luck there may even be snow.
The Arad Valley is less cold than Har Amasa in winter, but it can be very hot on hot days.

Water and food: there are several water points next to and around the trail: at the start of the route in the community of Har Amasa, near the trail in the village of Drijat, and near the trail in the Tel Arad National Park. The only place to buy food is in Arad, which offers many options. A meal can be arranged in advance in Drijat.
description_en:
The community of Har Amasa sits at the eastern edge of the Yatir Forest. Its entrance gate is usually closed, but you can ask to come in to fill up with water. It is worth chatting with the residents about life "at the end of the world" (even though in fact they are only a 40-minute drive from Be'er Sheva). The community began as a Nahal military settlement, became a kibbutz, and today is a small community settlement that takes in families.
The trail continues south from the community's gate, but it is recommended to first climb 200 m east to the northern viewpoint. From there you can continue south with the black markings and rejoin the trail.
After a kilometre we reach a viewpoint with the ruins of an ancient settlement - Khirbet Rujum Suweif. If the wind is not strong, this is a good spot for morning coffee and for a view over the southern Hebron Hills. After another kilometre of walking we reach the high viewpoint (841 m) - the Har Amasa lookout. You can read about the meaning of the name in the Bible, in the story of Absalom's revolt against David.
And while you are reading about David - go back to the story of Bathsheba and Nabal the Carmelite. The biblical Carmel and Maon area, where that story took place, is clearly visible from here looking north. Back then these were villages, small or large; today the whole area between Yatta, north of the Yatir Forest, and Hebron is one large built-up block. On a clear day there is a spectacular view from here over vast areas: from the mountains of Moab across the Jordan to Be'er Sheva and the plains of the Negev, and from Hebron to the Dimona hills.
From the viewpoint at the summit, the trail descends first south-west and then south. We descend about 300 m of elevation - over 3 km to the Dragot quarry.
North and south of the Har Amasa summit, the trail follows an ancient Roman road, which the Romans marked clearly with stones laid along both sides. Here and there ancient hewn steps can be seen. The road, called "Ma'ale Dragot" (not to be confused with the Dragot cliffs near Mitzpe Shalem), served among other things for the rapid movement of Roman army forces from the Hebron area to what was then the frontier, on the desert fringe.
Above the quarry, the Israel National Trail leaves the road, turns east and descends alongside a tributary of Nahal Kriyot to the Arad Valley. At the end of the descent we turn right onto a dirt road and walk to a road junction. At the junction we see to our right the construction and development works of a new neighbourhood being built at the foot of the village of Drijat.
At the junction we turn east (left), and after less than a kilometre we cross the wide channel of Nahal Kriyot; immediately after climbing out of the channel we turn south (right) onto a dirt road that runs along the edge of rain-fed fields. After a kilometre and a half, the Israel National Trail leaves the road, turns left and crosses the field alongside a gully cutting into the loess soil. Where the loess gully meets a main channel, we cross the channel and climb its eastern side on a dirt road. After a short walk on the road, the trail turns left and immediately right, and continues south on tracks between rain-fed fields until irrigated fields appear ahead of us. At the corner of the fields we turn and climb north to a prominent hill. From the top of the hill there is a view of Tel Arad; around the hill, the dark-brown iris blooms around March.
It is worth popping over to the Tel Arad National Park to fill up with water and rest. If you arrive in March - first check by phone with the national park whether the dark-brown iris is in bloom. If so, it is especially worth seeing; see details below.
The trail crosses Road 80 eastwards, the road that climbs from Tel Arad Junction to Har Amasa. We continue along the extensive fields of the Arad Valley, which belong to the communities of the southern Hebron Hills. Beside the large agricultural reservoir we turn south, and after a kilometre east again. From here we continue about 5 km east to the north-western corner of Arad. In the city you will find a variety of places to buy food (most are closed on Saturday). Arad's central bus station is just before Arad Junction, on the left.
nearby_en: A viewpoint from the community of Beit Yatir (Metzadot Yehuda), a 5-minute drive north of Har Amasa. The community's gate is closed and you have to wait for a local vehicle to arrive and open it. Drive up to the hill on the southern side of the community, park beside the building belonging to the pre-military academy and climb the external stairs to the roof of the building, which was built by the British.

The view south and east is wonderful; you can clearly see the edge of the Yatir Forest and understand an additional meaning of the term "Green Line". The name was indeed given because the border was drawn on the map in green pencil, but here the green of the forest stands out against the bare area north of the line. The community is one of the southern Hebron Hills settlements, but unlike most of them it lies south of the separation barrier.

The village of Drijat is the most special story in the area. A village that was "born" in the 19th century, when one of the fellahin of the Abu Hamed family fled from the southern Hebron Hills and lived in caves at the foot of "Ma'ale Dragot". The village developed as the only fellahin village in the area, separate from the Bedouin tribes, who regard the fellahin as an "inferior breed". Jaber, a resident of the village, has opened an impressive tourism business that includes a fascinating guided tour of the village, a visit to an old dwelling cave that has become a small visitors' centre, hospitality in a home and in a hospitality tent, meals and more. It is worth going in and touring the village independently as well.

Tel Arad National Park: all the information about the ancient city of Arad is provided in the national park's information sheet and film (entrance fee). The highlights of the visit are connected with the water works - a look into the ancient well at the bottom of the city and entry into the water reservoir in the Israelite fortress at the top of the hill. In addition, there is well-organised tent accommodation here, by prior arrangement.

The dark-brown iris bloom in the Arad Valley, near Tel Arad: the flowering time varies slightly from year to year. The peak is usually in mid-to-late March. It is worth checking with the Tel Arad National Park whether there is a bloom, which you can find by walking from the point where the trail meets the access road to Tel Arad, for 200-300 m south-west, to a low hill. On and around the hill you will see large concentrations of the beautiful dark iris and an abundance of other colourful flowers.

The Lebanon fritillary bloom in the Arad Valley: a charming and fairly rare flower that blooms here in large concentrations east of Road 80, north of the turn-off to Tel Arad, close to the flowering season of the dark-brown iris. For detailed information, it is recommended to consult the staff of the Tel Arad National Park.
author_en: Omer Shapira, Hiking Coordinator, Tourism Department, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI)
